q1: No — it is a markup language that describes structure and meaning. HTML has no execution engine, variables, or conditional logic. That is JavaScript's job.
q2: Structuring content and giving it semantic meaning is HTML's primary role. CSS handles presentation; JavaScript handles behaviour.
q3: WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) maintains the HTML Living Standard — a continuously evolving, single authoritative specification for HTML.
q4: Browser sends request → Server responds with HTML → Browser parses HTML and builds DOM → Browser paints page. This is the fundamental client-server request/render cycle.
q5: Hyper Text Markup Language. 'HyperText' refers to links that connect pages; 'Markup' means annotating content with tags; 'Language' is the syntax used to write it.
q6: An in-memory tree the browser builds from HTML, manipulable by JavaScript. The DOM (Document Object Model) is a live representation — JS can change it without editing the original file.
q7: Adding complex interactivity and logic is JavaScript's job. HTML's three roles are: providing semantic meaning, structuring documents, and embedding media content.
q8: False — HTML describes structure; CSS handles visual presentation. Mixing styling directly into HTML (e.g. using the deprecated <font> tag) is considered bad practice today.
q9: It identifies the location of a resource on the web for the browser to fetch. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) includes a scheme, domain, and path that together point to a specific resource.
q10: 2014 — when HTML5 became a W3C Recommendation. Since then the WHATWG Living Standard has been the primary evolving specification, with browsers implementing it continuously.
